To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
black and white men are more likely to be admitted to a forensic psychiatric hospital under the diagnosis of psychopathy if they have committed a violent offence.

black admission reports to a forensic hospital de-emphasize psychological states and stress external factors in explaining behaviour, whilst white admission reports reproduce traditional psychological models in which internal states are causally related to behaviour.

black men are underrepresented in the diagnosis of psychopathy, and this may be because they are less likely than whites to present with a model of the self which is consistent with the traditional psychological model of psychopathy.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the relationship between race and the psychological self.
the relationship between race, psychopathy, and the self.
how the psychological self is constructed and the implications that these constructions have for the experience of psychopathy.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the black and white men's admission reports articulate different models of the self.
black men are less likely to be diagnosed as psychopathic than white men because they do not articulate an internal psychological model of the psychopath.

the black reports devalue internal states and emphasize external influences, whilst the white reports do the reverse, and that these models are relevant to the experience and expression of psychopathy.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the black men's admission reports were more likely to include references to social and economic deprivation, and less likely to refer to psychological states such as anger and anxiety than the white men's reports.

we found that the black admission reports were more likely to emphasize the influence of the external world on the individual's psychological equilibrium, and to de-emphasize the role of internal states in influencing behaviour.

the black men were more likely to be diagnosed with personality disorder than psychopathy because they were more likely to articulate a model of the self that emphasized the importance of the external world and de-emphasized internal states.
The main takeaway from our work is that
black men are more likely to be diagnosed with a personality disorder rather than with a mental disorder.
the black and white men’s accounts of their experiences are not merely the product of individual pathology, but are shaped by the social and cultural context of the diagnostic category.

it is possible to identify implicit psychological models within the admission reports that are relevant to psychopathology and to the medico- legal classification of black and white patients as psychopaths.
